content: Acanthamoeba is a microscopic, single-celled organism classified as a free-living amoeba. It is capable of causing rare but severe infections in the eye, skin, and central nervous system. This amoeba is ubiquitously present in the environment, particularly in water and soil, and can be transmitted to humans through various routes. These include contact lens use, cuts or wounds on the skin, or inhalation into the lungs. Although most individuals are exposed to Acanthamoeba at some point in their lives, only a small fraction develop illness as a result of this exposure. Acanthamoeba is responsible for three distinct diseases: 1. Acanthamoeba Keratitis: This is an infection of the eye that typically occurs in otherwise healthy individuals. It can lead to severe complications, including permanent visual impairment or even blindness. 2. Granulomatous Amebic Encephalitis (GAE): This is a life-threatening infection of the brain and spinal cord. It is most commonly observed in individuals with compromised immune systems. 3. Disseminated Infection: This refers to a widespread infection that can involve multiple organ systems, including the skin, sinuses, lungs, and other internal organs. Disseminated infections are also more frequently seen in individuals with weakened immune defenses. The term ameba is used in U.S. English to describe this single-celled organism. However, the spelling amoeba is used in scientific genus names, such as Acanthamoeba, and is also the standard spelling in British English for both the generic organism and genus names. Acanthamoeba-related diseases are considered rare. In the United States, a rare disease is defined by the Rare Disease Act of 2002 as one that affects fewer than 200,000 individuals. This definition is also recognized by the National Institutes of Health and the Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Centers.
